message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical, Chemical, and Isotopic Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest of all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV | Energy to remove the single valence electron. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV | Energy released when an electron is added. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.44 K) | Extremely low; gaseous at room temperature. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Solidifies only at cryogenic temperatures. |
| **Density (at 25 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.00008988 g cm⁻³ | Very light; less dense than air. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas, 25 °C, 1 atm)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard for gas calculations. |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas | Diatomic molecules (H₂). |
| **Molecular weight of H₂** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ | Two hydrogen atoms per molecule. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy required to break the H₂ bond. |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar) | H₂ is a homonuclear diatomic molecule. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series | Hydrogen’s emission/absorption lines are fundamental in astrophysics. |
| **Isotopes** |  |  |
| • ¹H (protium) | 99.98 % | One proton, no neutrons. |
| • ²H (deuterium) | 0.02 % | One proton, one neutron. |
| • ³H (tritium) | <10⁻⁶ % | One proton, two neutrons; radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.32 y). |
| **Chemical behavior** |  |  |
| • Reactivity** | Highly reactive with many elements; forms hydrides (e.g., NaH, CaH₂). |
| • Acid–base** | Acts as a weak acid (HX → H⁺ + X⁻) in aqueous solution. |
| • Oxidation states** | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride). |
| • Bonding** | Forms covalent bonds (H₂), ionic bonds (NaH), and hydrogen bonds (in water). |
| **Physical uses** |  |  |
| • Fuel** | Hydrogen fuel cells produce electricity with water as the only by‑product. |
| • Industrial** | Used in ammonia synthesis (Haber process), petroleum refining, and as a reducing agent. |
| • Spacecraft** | Liquid hydrogen used as rocket propellant (e.g., Space Shuttle). |
| **Astrophysical significance** |  |  |
| • Stellar fusion** | Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium in stars, releasing energy (E=mc²). |
| • **Cosmology** | Primordial hydrogen constitutes ~75 % of baryonic matter. |
| **Safety considerations** |  |  |
| • Flammability** | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂ in air). |
| • Toxicity** | Non‑toxic, but can displace oxygen in confined spaces, leading to asphyxiation. |
| • Cryogenic hazards** | Liquid hydrogen is extremely cold (–253 °C); can cause frostbite or material embrittlement. |

---

### Quick Reference Summary

- **Atomic number:** 1  
- **Common isotope:** ¹H (protium)  
- **Molecular form at STP:** H₂ (diatomic gas)  
- **Boiling point:** –252.9 °C (20 K)  
- **Density:** 0.0000899 g cm⁻³  
- **Electronegativity:** 2.20  
- **Ionization energy:** 13.6 eV  
- **Key uses:** fuel cells, rocket propellant, industrial hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis.  
- **Astrophysical role:** fuel for stellar fusion, major component of the universe’s baryonic matter.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property (e.g., spectroscopic lines, isotopic chemistry, or applications in energy technology).
